title: Walking After Ten. The Town Sounds Different and So Do My Thoughts
body: The route is the same one I walk at noon. Down the hill, past the bakery, around the small park with the broken fountain, back up through the alley with the cats. At ten at night it is a different street wearing the same clothes. The first thing that changes is ownership. At noon the sidewalk belongs to errands. Everyone is going somewhere for a reason, and I am going somewhere for a reason, and we are all slight obstacles to one another. At ten the sidewalk is mostly mine. The few people out are walking dogs or smoking on balconies or closing shutters, and there is a nod we exchange that I can only describe as shift change. The night walkers have taken over the building. The second thing is sound. At noon the town is one loud sentence. At night it is individual words. A bottle somewhere. The fountain, which at noon is broken and at night is dripping, patiently, a sound that was always there and needed the silence to exist. My own footsteps, which embarrass me slightly at noon and at night become a rhythm I can think inside. And that is the real discovery. My thoughts have a daytime voice and a nighttime voice. The daytime voice is fast and useful and loop-heavy. It rehearses the conversation from Tuesday. The nighttime voice, fed by dark and rhythm and low stimulus, is slower and stranger and strangely kinder. Problems I have been chewing for hours at a desk soften at the tenth minute of a night walk. Not solved, necessarily. Softened. Made walkable. There is a physiological explanation I half remember about dark and movement and the default mode network, and I do not care to look it up carefully, because the mechanism is not the point. The point is availability. The night walk is the only appointment my own head keeps with me regularly. The phone stays in the pocket. The streets are empty enough that boredom becomes possible, and boredom, it turns out, is where some of my better thinking was hiding all along, waiting for me to stop being interesting. The cats have a union and I am not in it. The alley cats permit noon walkers and night walkers but enforce different rules. At noon they are professionals, indifferent, positioned. At night a small orange one walks with me for half a block at a fixed distance, like a colleague who prefers not to talk. I have come to value this. Company without obligation is rare at any hour. Practical notes, since people ask. Same route, not new routes. New routes at night turn the walk into navigation and navigation eats the thinking. Headphone in one ear only, audiobook at low speed, or nothing. Nothing is better. Twelve minutes minimum before judging the walk, because the first twelve minutes are spent by the mind emptying its pockets. The bakery is closed but the smell of tomorrow's bread is already working. The fountain drips. Somewhere above, a window is blue with television light. The street I thought I knew introduces itself again, quieter, and I get to meet it as a person rather than as a schedule. Then the hill up, which is honest about being a hill, and the door, and the bed, and sleep that arrives like a tide instead of a collapse. Noon belongs to the world. Ten at night belongs to the route.
